ABSTRACT 
Continuous, real-time monitoring of indoor environmental conditions —specifically ambient temperature, 
relative atmospheric humidity, and airborne gaseous contaminants —is vital for ensuring human 
respiratory safety, occupational productivity, and building ventilation efficiency. This report details the 
comprehensive design, virtual simulation, embedded firmware architecture, physical hardware realization, 
and metrological validation of an autonomous, low -cost environmental monitoring station powered by an 
8-bit ATmega328P microcontroller on the Arduino Uno platform. 
The project adopts a dual -phase implementation strategy. In the virtual prototyping phase, an interactive 
circuit simulation was modeled within Autodesk Tinkercad Circuits, combining an analog TMP36 
temperature transducer, a six -terminal heated gas sensor model, and a 16x2 alphanumeric liquid crystal 
display interfaced via an Adafruit I2C backpack. C++ firmware was formulated to linearize sensor 
voltages and categorize gas responses across a multi-tier qualitative threshold logic. 
In the subsequent physical implementation phase, the system was physically fabricated on an 830 -tie-
point solderless breadboard. The thermal channel was upgraded to a digital DHT11 composite sensor, 
delivering simultaneous temperature (0 –50°C) and relative humidity (20 –90% RH) telemetry over a 
single-bus digital protocol. The gas channel was populated with a commercial MQ -135 metal oxide 
semiconductor breakout module utilizing Tin Dioxide (SnO2) chemiresistive surface adsorption. Visual 
feedback is rendered  locally on a 16x2 LCD via a PCF8574 I2C adapter, supplemented by diagnostic 
serial telemetry streamed at 9600 baud.

1.1 The Imperative for Modern Environmental Monitoring 
In an era marked by rapid industrialization, dense urbanization, and increasing climate variability, the 
continuous observation and real -time assessment of environmental parameters have transitioned from 
specialized meteorological pursuits into essential public health, occupational safety, and residential well -
being priorities. The atmosphere within our immediate living, educational, and working spaces exerts a 
direct, quantifiable influence on human physiology, cognitive focus, respiratory health, and over all 
comfort. Parameters such as ambient temperature, relative humidity, and the ambient concentration of 
noxious gases, volatile chemical compounds, and airborne combustion byproducts govern both acute 
physical sensations and long-term biological outcomes. 
Historically, environmental data collection relied predominantly on bulky, prohibitively expensive, and 
centralized laboratory -grade measurement stations operated by municipal agencies or industrial 
conglomerates. While these flagship installations achieve exceptional analytical precision and comply 
strictly with federal reference standards, their substantial capital cost, complex maintenance regimens, 
and physical scarcity create substantial spatial and temporal data voids. A municipal monitoring station 
positioned five kilometers away from an academic building or indoor laboratory provides virtually no 
actionable intelligence regarding localized toxic vapor buildup, sudden thermal spikes caused by 
equipment overheating, or stagnant ventilation pockets within individual architectural enclosures. 
To bridge this fundamental resolution gap, modern instrumentation engineering increasingly embraces 
decentralized, micro -scale sensor architectures. The emergence of open -source computing platforms, 
ubiquitous microcontrollers, and mass-manufactured solid-state transducers has catalyzed a democratizing 
revolution across environmental telemetry. Compact, low -power embedded monitoring stations can now 
be fabricated and deployed at a minor fraction of traditional costs, enabling hyper -local, continuous 
tracking of microclimates and internal air masses. 
This project details the systematic conceptualization, virtual simulation, algorithmic development, and 
physical realization of an autonomous, Arduino -based environmental monitoring station. Specifically 
engineered to track ambient temperature, relative humidity, and broad-spectrum gaseous responses in real 
time, the system balances pedagogical transparency with rigorous engineering execution, delivering 
instantaneous visual feedback through a standardized liquid -crystal interface while logging serial 
diagnostic telemetry for in-depth data interrogation.

Topic 3: Theoretical Foundations and Technical Concepts 
3.1 Architecture of Embedded Microcontroller Systems 
An embedded system represents an integrated computational assembly of hardware processing silicon, 
specialized memory hierarchies, peripheral input/output circuitry, and dedicated control software 
designed to execute an unbroken deterministic sequence of real -time tasks. In stark contrast to general -
purpose desktop computing systems that run multi -tasking operating systems with arbitrary scheduling 
and high power dissipation, embedded microcontroller units (MCUs) are engineered for direct physical 
interaction with the electrical domain. 
At the core of the Arduino Uno R3 development board resides the Microchip (formerly Atmel) 
ATmega328P—an 8-bit high-performance AVR enhanced RISC architecture microcontroller. Operating 
at a crystal-stabilized clock frequency of 16 MHz, the ATmega328P achieves throughputs approaching 16 
MIPS (Million Instructions Per Second) by executing powerful single -clock-cycle instructions. The 
silicon die integrates 32 Kilobytes of in -system self -programmable Flash memory for firmware 
instruction storage, 2 Kilobytes of static Random Access Memory (SRAM) for runtime dynamic variable 
allocation, and 1 Kilobyte of Electrically Erasable Programmable Read -Only Memory (EEPROM) for 
non-volatile parameter retention. 
The functional bridge between the digital logic core and external environmental sensors is provided by 
the internal peripheral controllers: General Purpose Input/Output (GPIO) registers, hardware 
timer/counters, a programmable UART serial engine, a Two-Wire Interface (TWI/I2C) hardware module, 
and an integrated multi-channel Analog-to-Digital Converter. 
3.2 Transducers and Physical Sensing Principles 
In measurement and instrumentation science, a transducer is formally defined as any physical device that 
transforms an input energy or variable belonging to one physical domain into a corresponding, 
measurable signal in another domain —almost universally the electrical domain. Environmental 
transducers encompass two distinct operational subclasses: sensors and actuators. Sensors serve as input 
transducers, converting thermodynamic, optical, acoustic, or chemical variations into measurable 
voltages, currents, or impedance changes. 
The physical transducers employed in this monitoring platform represent distinct transducer 
classifications. The TMP36 temperature sensor utilizes solid -state semiconductor physics, exploiting the 
temperature-dependent base-emitter junction voltage (Vbe) differential of forward -biased silicon bipolar 
transistors. In contrast, the MQ -135 chemical sensor relies upon surface adsorption chemistry on 
polycrystalline metal-oxide semiconductors (specifically Tin Dioxide, SnO2), where gaseous molecules 
alter electrical conduction through donor electron transfer. Finally, the DHT11 sensor pairs a negative 
temperature coefficient (NTC) thermistor with a capacitive humidity polymer whose dielectric 
permittivity fluctuates in direct thermodynamic equilibrium with ambient water vapor molecules. 
3.3 Principles of Analog-to-Digital Conversion (ADC) 
Because physical phenomena such as temperature and chemical concentration manifest as continuous 
analog variables across infinite voltage spectra, an analog -to-digital converter is required to discretize 
these signals into finite digital representations that an 8 -bit digital processing core can manipulate. The

ATmega328P incorporates an internal 10 -bit Successive Approximation Register (SAR) ADC connected 
through an internal analog multiplexer to six external pins (designated A0 through A5). 
Quantization Resolution: A 10 -bit binary representation subdivides the operational voltage reference 
spectrum into 2^10 = 1024 discrete quantized voltage increments (steps ranging numerically from 0 to 
1023). When utilizing the default reference configuration, the ADC is tied directly to the positive 5.0 V 
microcontroller system supply rail (Vcc). Consequently, the fundamental step size —known as the Least 
Significant Bit (LSB) voltage resolution—is mathematically determined as: 
V_LSB = V_ref / (2^10 - 1) = 5.000 V / 1023 ≈ 0.0048876 V (4.888 mV per count) 
To convert an observed integer ADC quantization count (ADC_val) back into its equivalent physical 
input voltage (V_in), the firmware applies the standard transfer equation: 
V_in = ADC_val * (V_ref / 1023.0) 
Systemic Error Considerations: While theoretically straightforward, practical ADC quantization in 
breadboard environments is susceptible to multiple real -world error sources. Fluctuations in the USB 
supply voltage (which frequently dips to 4.75 V or surges to 5.20 V depending on computer host load) 
directly skew V_ref, producing proportional percentage errors in raw voltage calculations. Furthermore, 
input source impedance exceeding 10 kΩ, thermal noise across breadboard spring contacts, and lack of 
external ceramic bypass capacitors can cause sample-and-hold capacitor settling errors during rapid multi-
channel analog switching. 
3.4 The Inter-Integrated Circuit (I2C) Protocol 
Parallel alphanumeric displays historically required up to 16 physical electrical conductors, demanding at 
least 6 dedicated microcontroller GPIO pins for basic 4 -bit data transfers (Register Select, Enable, and 
data lines D4 -D7). In microcontroller platforms with constrained pin counts, this parallel overhead 
exhausts available inputs. To solve this dilemma, the instrumentation system utilizes the Inter -Integrated 
Circuit (I2C) serial bus protocol developed by Philips Semiconductor (now NXP). 
The I2C bus utilizes a synchronous, multi -master, multi-slave, bidirectional serial architecture requiring 
only two active signal lines alongside common power and ground rails: Serial Data (SDA) and Serial 
Clock (SCL). Both SDA and SCL are designed with open -drain/open-collector outputs pulled high to the 
positive supply rail through external pull -up resistors (typically 4.7 kΩ to 10 kΩ). On the Arduino Uno 
R3, hardware I2C peripheral lines are mapped physically to analog pins A4 (SDA) and A5 (SCL), as well 
as duplicated on dedicated header pins adjacent to AREF. 
Data transmission proceeds via byte -framed packet transfers governed strictly by the clock signal 
generated by the master (Arduino). Communication begins with a START condition (SDA pulled LOW 
while SCL remains HIGH), followed by a 7 -bit slave address byte, a Read/Write direction bit, an 
Acknowledge (ACK/NACK) bit from the peripheral, one or more 8 -bit data payload bytes, and a STOP 
condition (SDA released HIGH while SCL remains HIGH). In this project, an on -board PCF8574 8 -bit 
remote I/O expander chip moun ted to the rear of the LCD decodes the I2C serial stream and drives the 
parallel HD44780 display controller with zero pin waste on the Arduino.

3.5 Comparative Analysis: Simulation vs. Physical Hardware 
A foundational lesson emphasized throughout this project is that computer -based Electronic Design 
Automation (EDA) simulations represent highly idealized behavioral abstractions rather than complete 
physical replicas. While web -based simulation platforms such as Autodesk Tinkercad Circuits provide 
immense instructional value for verifying schematic routing, testing conditional logic, and debugging 
display formatting without risk of component burnout, real -world hardware manifests physical 
complexities that simulations fundamentally omit. 
In simulation, internal resistance in connecting jumper wires is modeled as precisely zero; supply rails 
never experience ripple or sag; analog sensors exhibit instantaneous thermal equilibrium without response 
latency; and environmental noise is virtually absent. In physical hardware, ambient thermal gradients, 
stray parasitic capacitance, mechanical vibration across breadboard contacts, atmospheric humidity 
variations, and chemical sensor heater warm-up cycles profoundly influence signal stability. Recogn izing 
and designing robust firmware to accommodate these physical phenomena represents a core milestone of 
real-world instrumentation engineering. 
Metrological Insight: Simulation proves functional logic; physical prototyping validates environmental 
physics. High ADC precision on a computer screen cannot compensate for supply rail fluctuations or 
uncalibrated sensor cross-sensitivities on a physical breadboard.

Topic 6: Transducer Physics and Environmental Sensor Principles 
6.1 Analog Thermal Transducer: TMP36 Precision Sensor 
The TMP36 is a low-voltage, precision centigrade temperature sensor fabricated by Analog Devices. The 
device operates on the fundamental physical principle of the silicon bandgap temperature sensor, 
exploiting the predictable thermodynamic relationship governing the base -emitter voltage difference 
(ΔVbe) between two identical bipolar transistors operating at differing collector current densities. This 
differential voltage is inherently proportional to absolute temperature in Kelvin (PTAT - Proportional to 
Absolute Temperature). 
Internal signal conditioning circuitry linearizes and amplifies this core thermal voltage, producing an 
analog output that is directly proportional to temperature in degrees Celsius. Crucially, the TMP36 
incorporates an intentional 500 mV (0.50 V) DC offset at 0°C. This deliberate offset allows the sensor to 
measure negative temperatures down to -40°C without requiring a negative dual -rail power supply. The 
output voltage scaling factor is exactly 10.0 mV/°C. Consequently, the mathematical transfer function  
converting measured output voltage (V_out) into temperature (T_C) is expressed as: 
T_C = (V_out - 0.500 V) * 100 °C/V 
For example, when the sensor is exposed to a nominal room temperature of 25.0°C, the output pin 
produces an electrical potential of: V_out = 0.500 V + (25.0 * 0.010 V) = 0.750 V. The sensor operates 
over a broad supply voltage span of 2.7 V to 5.5 V, consumes less than 50 µA of quiescent current, and 
exhibits low self -heating (less than 0.1°C in still air), making it an exceptional thermal reference in 
simulation and introductory physical laboratories. 
6.2 Digital Environmental Transducer: DHT11 Temperature & Relative Humidity 
Sensor 
The DHT11 is an integrated composite environmental sensor module manufactured by Aosong 
Electronics, capable of delivering calibrated digital output for both temperature and relative humidity. 
The module incorporates two distinct physical transducers paired with an internal 8 -bit OTP (One -Time

Relative humidity measurement is performed via a resistive -capacitive humidity sensing component. The

Simultaneously, temperature is measured via an integrated Negative Temperature Coefficient (NTC)

The onboard microcontroller continuously measures these elements, looks up factory calibration

milliseconds, followed by a 20 -40 microsecond HIGH pull -up. The DHT11 responds with an 80 
microsecond LOW acknow ledgement, followed by 40 consecutive data bits: 16 bits of humidity data 
(integer and decimal), 16 bits of temperature data (integer and decimal), and an 8 -bit checksum byte that 
guarantees communication integrity. 
6.3 Chemiresistive Metal-Oxide Gas Transducer: MQ-135 Sensor 
The MQ-135 is a broad -spectrum chemiresistive gas sensor belonging to the widely utilized MQ family 
manufactured by Zhengzhou Winsen Electronics. The core sensing element consists of a micro -machined 
ceramic tube (Al2O3) coated with a thin polycrystalline layer of Tin Dioxide (SnO2), enclosing an 
internal Nickel -Chromium (Ni -Cr) resistance heating coil. The sensor operates on the fundamental 
physical chemistry of high-temperature gas adsorption and surface redox reactions. 
When the internal heater coil is energized with a continuous 5.0 V DC supply, the SnO2 sensing layer is 
heated to its optimal operating temperature of approximately 300°C to 400°C. In clean ambient air, 
atmospheric oxygen molecules adsorb onto the crystalline surfaces of the Tin Dioxide particles, capturing 
conduction-band donor electrons to form negatively charged chemisorbed oxygen ions (O- and O2-). This 
electron trapping creates a significant potential energy barrier between adjacent crystal grains, resulting in 
high baseline electrical resistance (R0). 
When the heated sensor encounters reducing gases or target volatile pollutants —such as carbon dioxide 
(CO2), ammonia (NH3), benzene (C6H6), alcohol vapors, or smoke —these gaseous molecules undergo 
oxidation reactions with the chemisorbed surface oxygen ions. This redox reaction releases the trapped 
donor electrons back into the SnO2 conduction band, dramatically reducing the inter -granular potential 
barrier and causing the bulk electrical resistance of the sensing layer (Rs) to drop substantially. 
The physical breakout module integrates a precision load resistor (RL, typically 10 kΩ to 47 kΩ) in series 
with the variable sensor element (Rs), forming a classic voltage divider network. As target gas 
concentrations rise and Rs falls, the voltage drop across the load resistor (V_RL) increases proportionally 
according to the voltage divider equation: V_RL = Vcc * [RL / (Rs + RL)]. This analog voltage is 
exposed on the AO pin and routed directly to the Arduino ADC.

6.4 Chemiresistive Dynamics, Calibration Imperatives, and Honest Metrology 
While metal -oxide semiconductor (MOS) sensors provide exceptional sensitivity at minimal cost, 
professional engineering demands a thorough understanding of their physical constraints and metrological 
realities: 
• Mandatory Thermal Preheating (Burn -In): Metal -oxide sensors require an initial burn -in stabilization 
period of 24 to 48 hours of continuous heater operation to burn off manufacturing chemical residues. 
Furthermore, whenever powered on from a cold state, the sensor requires a warm -up stabilization phase 
of 2 to 5 minutes before electrical resistance reaches dynamic equilibrium. 
• Atmospheric Cross -Sensitivity: The MQ -135 lacks chemical selectivity. It responds concurrently to 
ammonia, carbon dioxide, ethanol, acetone, carbon monoxide, and cigarette smoke. A sudden spike in 
sensor voltage may indicate alcohol vapors from an antiseptic wipe rather than hazardous air pollution. 
• Environmental Dependency (Temperature & Humidity Skew): The rate of surface gas adsorption is 
strongly influenced by ambient temperature and relative humidity. High humidity causes water vapor 
molecules to compete with oxygen for adsorption sites, artificially depressing sensor resistance. True 
scientific accuracy requires mathematical temperature/humidity compensation curves derived from 
manufacturer datasheets. 
• Honest Metrological Labelling: In student and hobbyist projects, raw MQ -135 ADC values are 
frequently mislabeled as 'Air Pollution Percentage' or 'Certified Air Quality Index (AQI)'. This practice is 
scientifically invalid. Formal AQI is a federally standardized metric governed by complex multi-pollutant 
epidemiological formulas measuring PM2.5, PM10, O3, NO2, SO2, and CO over multi -hour running 
averages. In this project, the gas response is strictly and honestly classified as an arbitrary 'Classroom 
Demonstration Response Scale (0 -100)'. This transparent terminology maintains absolute scientific and 
academic integrity.

Topic 9: Firmware Architecture, Algorithmic Design, and Flow Control 
9.1 Structural Execution Philosophy and Timing Architecture 
Embedded firmware architecture fundamentally dictates the reliability, responsiveness, and long -term 
stability of an instrumentation device. In traditional beginner -level Arduino code, developers rely heavily 
upon the blocking delay() function to pace program execution and control LCD refresh rates. However, 
invoking delay(3000) completely halts the ATmega328P processor core for three seconds, suspending 
serial communications, preventing real -time error handling, and making responsive multi -tasking 
impossible. 
To overcome these critical limitations, the firmware for this environmental monitoring system is 
structured around a non -blocking cooperative state scheduler utilizing the microcontroller's hardware 
Timer0 millisecond counter (millis()). The main loop executes continuously at full clock speed, querying 
whether the elapsed time since the prior operational cycle has surpassed a preconfigured threshold (const 
unsigned long updateInterval = 3000 ms). This ensures that background tasks, serial buffer monitoring,  
and error watchdogs operate with zero latency while sensor sampling and screen refreshes occur 
deterministically. 
9.2 Mathematical Quantization, Normalization, and Mapping Algorithms 
Raw digital data acquired from embedded transducers requires multi -stage mathematical transformation 
before it can be presented meaningfully to human operators: 
Stage 1: Analog Quantization to True Voltage: When analog channels are sampled via analogRead(), the 
10-bit ADC yields an integer count ranging from 0 to 1023. The firmware normalizes this count into true 
floating-point voltage using the formula: float voltage = (float)adcCount * (5.0 / 1023.0). 
Stage 2: Thermal Linearization (TMP36): For analog temperature conversion, the 0.50 V offset is 
subtracted and the result multiplied by 100: float temperature = (voltage - 0.50) * 100.0. 
Stage 3: Chemical Sensor Mapping: The raw gas ADC value (0 -1023) is translated onto a normalized 
demonstration response scale (0 -100) using the integer scaling function: int responseScale = 
map(gasRaw, 0, 1023, 0, 100); followed by mathematical bounding: responseScale = 
constrain(responseScale, 0, 100); to guarantee array index safety and prevent overflow bugs.

Because raw metal -oxide sensor outputs reflect broad -spectrum relative resistance changes rather than 
calibrated chemical concentrations, presenting unvarnished numbers to non -technical users creates

• Tier 1 (Response Scale 0 to 29): Categorized as 'GOOD'. Represents normal, clean ambient baseline 
conditions with minimal detected reducing gases or volatile airborne contaminants. 
• Tier 2 (Response Scale 30 to 59): Categorized as 'MODERATE'. Reflects slight atmospheric variations, 
elevated human occupancy, minor stagnation in room air, or trace volatile compounds. 
• Tier 3 (Response Scale 60 to 79): Categorized as 'POOR'. Indicates noticeable accumulation of organic 
vapors, cooking fumes, stagnant respiratory CO2, or soldering smoke requiring active ventilation. 
• Tier 4 (Response Scale 80 to 100): Categorized as 'DANGER'. Signifies heavy localized chemical 
fumes, combustible gas leakage, or intense smoke saturation demanding immediate room evacuation. 
These boundaries represent pedagogical demonstration thresholds designed to demonstrate conditional 
state-machine logic in classroom laboratories, explicitly distinguishing them from federally mandated 
regulatory air quality standards. 
9.4 Robust Error Trapping, Sensor Validation, and Fault Recovery 
A hallmark of professional -grade firmware is graceful error handling. When interfacing digital 
transducers such as the DHT11, communication timeouts, loose breadboard jumpers, or electrical noise 
can corrupt the 40 -bit data stream, causing library functions to return IEEE NaN (Not -a-Number) 
floating-point flags. 
Rather than crashing or printing unreadable garbage characters to the LCD, the firmware actively traps 
these conditions using the isnan(temperature) || isnan(humidity) macro. If a communication fault is 
detected, the firmware suppresses downstream arithmetic, outputs an explicit diagnostic warning ('DHT11 
read error') to the display, logs the fault over the UART serial stream, and executes an immediate loop 
return, waiting for the subsequent sampling interval to attempt self-recovery.

pin A4 and SCL to analog pin A5.

scanner sketch to verify that the backpack responds at expected address 0x27 or 0x3F. Adjust the blue

GND to Ground, and route the DATA pin to Arduino digital pin D2.

11.3 Electrical Power Distribution, Heater Current Dissipation, and Thermal 
Management 
A critical physical consideration in multi -sensor embedded design is total electrical current consumption. 
While standard digital sensors like the DHT11 consume less than 2.5 mA during active measurements, 
the MQ-135 utilizes an internal resistive heating element (31 Ω ±3 Ω) that consumes approximately 150 
mA to 180 mA of continuous current at 5.0 V DC. 
When combined with the Arduino microcontroller core (~50 mA) and the 16x2 LCD LED backlight (~30 
mA), the complete physical instrument draws approximately 240 mA to 270 mA. While well within the 
500 mA current limit of standard USB 2.0 computer ports, powering the circuit from unpowered USB 
hubs or undersized 9V alkaline batteries through the onboard 5V regulator can cause regulator thermal 
overload and voltage brownouts. A dedicated 5V 1A regulated USB power source or USB 3.0 port is 
strongly recommended for continuous benchtop operation.

address is the single most common cause of blank LCD screens in student laboratories.

14.2 Physical Limitations and Environmental Cross-Sensitivity Analysis 
Rigorous engineering requires explicit recognition of physical sensor limitations and measurement 
boundaries:

• Transducer Resolution & Accuracy Bounds: The DHT11 sensor utilizes an 8 -bit internal ADC, limiting 
temperature resolution to whole 1°C increments and humidity to 1% RH steps. For critical meteorological 
or industrial cleanroom applications, a more refined sensor such as the DHT22 (0.1°C resolution) or 
Sensirion SHT35 would be required. 
• Chemiresistive Non-Selectivity: The MQ-135 is inherently non-selective. It responds to broad classes of 
reducing gases and organic vapors. The instrument cannot distinguish between hazardous carbon 
monoxide, harmless cooking steam, or hand sanitizer vapors. It functions strictly as an aggregate air 
quality change indicator rather than a selective gas chromatograph. 
• Metrological Classification Boundaries: As emphasized throughout this study, the mapped 0 -100 
response scale is an arbitrary demonstration metric. It must never be represented as certified Air Quality 
Index (AQI) or specific particulate matter (PM2.5/PM10) concentrations. 
• Thermal Drift in Enclosed Spaces: The internal heating element of the MQ-135 operates continuously at 
~350°C, dissipating radiant heat into the surrounding air. If housed in a compact, poorly ventilated 
physical enclosure, this localized heater can artificially raise ambient temperature readings on the nearby 
DHT11 by 1.5°C to 3.0°C. Physical isolation baffles are mandatory in permanent enclosures. 
14.3 Operational Safety Precautions and Benchtop Hazard Management 
Operating heated electrochemical instrumentation on a student laboratory bench entails specific electrical 
and thermal safety obligations: 
1. High -Temperature Surface Hazard: The stainless steel mesh capsule of the MQ -135 becomes 
noticeably warm during operation (surface temperatures reach 50°C to 65°C). Never touch the metal 
mesh during or immediately following active operation. 
2. Flammable Atmosphere Restrictions: Do not expose the heated MQ-135 sensor to concentrated streams 
of flammable gases (such as pure butane from a lighter or concentrated ether). The internal heater coil 
represents a potential ignition source in explosive atmospheres. 
3. Power Bus Short-Circuit Prevention: Always disconnect USB power prior to modifying jumper wires. 
Accidental shorts between the 5.0 V power rail and Ground can blow the Arduino onboard polyfuse or 
damage host computer USB ports. 
4. Chemical Safety: When testing sensor response to solvents or alcohol, perform tests in a well -
ventilated laboratory space, using sterile swabs rather than pouring open liquid containers over 
breadboard electronics. 
Safety Mandate: Never use this educational prototype as a primary safety alarm, life-support monitor, or 
certified hazardous gas leak detector. It is designed exclusively for educational demonstration and 
ambient laboratory tracking.
